interactions.label: What is the fundamental difference between surgical audit and clinical research?

params.question: What is the fundamental difference between surgical audit and clinical research?

answers.text: Audit measures current practice against an existing standard, while research tests a hypothesis to generate new knowledge

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Audit asks 'are we meeting the standard we already accept?' Research asks 'what should the standard be?' This distinction drives all three practical consequences — governance, the type of conclusions drawn, and generalisability.

answers.text: Audit requires prior ethics committee approval, while research does not

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect — this reverses the actual relationship. Research on human participants requires ethics committee approval and informed consent. Audit, which simply measures practice against an existing standard, generally does not.

answers.text: Audit generates knowledge that is generalisable beyond the local setting, while research findings apply only locally

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect — this is the reverse. Well-designed research aims to produce generalisable knowledge. Audit findings belong to the specific unit audited.

answers.text: Audit tests whether a new intervention causes better outcomes, while research compares outcomes with national data

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect — the two activities are swapped here. Testing a new intervention is research. Comparing outcomes against a known national standard is audit.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key distinction is this: audit measures practice against an existing standard ('are we doing what we know works?'), while research tests a hypothesis to create new knowledge ('what should best practice be?'). This determines governance requirements, the strength of conclusions, and generalisability.

Well done. This core distinction — existing standard versus new hypothesis — is what determines whether ethics approval is needed, what conclusions can be drawn, and whether findings apply beyond the local unit.

params.question: A colleague argues that their cross-sectional study of 10,000 patients provides stronger evidence than a randomised controlled trial of 200 patients. Based on the hierarchy of evidence, which response is most accurate?

answers.text: The colleague is correct because larger sample sizes always produce stronger evidence

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While sample size affects precision, it is the study design — particularly the use of randomisation to control confounding — that determines how credible a causal conclusion can be.

answers.text: The colleague is incorrect because study design, not sample size, determines the strength of evidence

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Randomisation in an RCT controls both known and unknown confounders across groups — a property no observational design can match, regardless of how many participants it includes. That is why the RCT sits above observational designs in the hierarchy.

answers.text: The colleague is correct because cross-sectional studies sit above randomised trials in the hierarchy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Cross-sectional studies sit below randomised controlled trials in the hierarchy. They measure prevalence at a single point in time and cannot establish which came first — the exposure or the outcome.

answers.text: Both designs produce equally strong evidence provided the statistical analysis is rigorous

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Rigorous statistical analysis cannot compensate for fundamental design limitations. A cross-sectional study remains susceptible to confounding and cannot establish temporality, regardless of how sophisticated the analysis.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key insight from the hierarchy of evidence is this: it is the design, not the sample size, that determines how credible a conclusion is. Randomisation in an RCT balances both known and unknown confounders — no observational design, however large, can achieve this.

Exactly right. Design determines the ceiling of evidence. A well-conducted RCT with 200 participants can establish causation more convincingly than an observational study of 10,000 because randomisation controls confounding in a way no observational method can.

interactions.label: A surgical unit compares its 30-day mortality after emergency laparotomy against

params.question: A surgical unit compares its 30-day mortality after emergency laparotomy against the national benchmark published by a surgical outcomes registry. After finding a higher-than-expected rate, the team introduces a perioperative care bundle and plans to remeasure after six months. This project is best classified as:

answers.text: Clinical research, because it introduces a new care bundle as an intervention

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Introducing change is a normal part of the audit cycle — it closes the gap between current practice and the standard. The deciding feature is that the team measures against an existing national benchmark, not a new hypothesis.

answers.text: A cohort study, because it follows patient outcomes over time

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A cohort study is an observational research design that follows groups with different exposures forward in time to measure incidence. This project measures unit performance against a published standard, which is the hallmark of audit, not research.

answers.text: Surgical audit, because it compares practice against an existing standard and plans a re-audit to close the cycle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. All hallmarks of the audit cycle are present: an existing external standard (national benchmark), measurement of actual practice, identification of a gap, implementation of change, and a plan to re-audit. No hypothesis is being tested.

answers.text: A randomised controlled trial, because it compares outcomes before and after introducing the care bundle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A randomised controlled trial requires random allocation of participants to intervention and control groups. This project has no randomisation, no control group, and no hypothesis — it measures practice against a known standard and acts to close the gap.

overallFeedback.feedback: The deciding feature is whether the work tests a new hypothesis or measures practice against an existing standard. This project uses a national benchmark as the standard, identifies a gap, implements change, and plans to re-audit — all hallmarks of the audit cycle, not research. Introducing change does not make an activity research.

Well done. The deciding feature is always whether the work measures against an existing standard (audit) or tests a hypothesis to generate new knowledge (research). Here, the national benchmark provides the standard, and the re-measurement closes the audit cycle.
